Flying from Lisbon to Marseilles
January 15, 1940
Dear Family:
I left Baltimore last Sunday, January 7th, on the American Clipper.
arrived at Bermuda after a fast flight of only four and one half hours.
However, on our arrival we learned that high seas at our next stop,
Horta, Azores, prevented a landing there.
The next three days, i.e. the 8th,
th and on for better.
weather at Horta.
We did a lot of bicycling at
Bermuda and one day rode
twenty miles. My legs felt like a toe-dancer's look!
Finally on January llth we left for Horta and flew all night, arriving
too late, however, to make lisbon before dark.
We stayed overnight at
the "Pan
American Mess" - a very well built and comfortable building
constructed originally for Western Union in the old days when all cables
had to be relayed by hand sending. Now, of course, all messages are
transmitted by machine and W.U. have no need for most of the quarters
which they formerly required.
the next day, January 13th, the weather
was impossible, and
as a result I had two full days at Horta, which
worked out well for me because I had planned to spend that much time
there on my way over or coming back.
We left Horta on the morning of the 14th and arrived at Lisbon around
4:00 o'clock in the afternoon. I was met there by an old friend from
Macao, Lieut. Costa, and, oi
course, was delighted to see him.
late into the night, or rather morning, with our Lisbon
represen-
tative and wrote a report
to New York, finally getting to bed at 3:00
a.m. with a call for 5:00 a.m.
as I write, it is 8:45 a.m. and with four other Clipper passengers
I am flying in a French airplane south along the Portugese coast.
left Lisbon an hour ago and soon we'll fly by Gibraltar and across to
Oran, Algeria. It seems ridiculous to fly from Lisbon to Marseilles
via Africa,
but the French can not secure rights to fly over Spain and
so avoid doing so while yet connecting Algeria with France.
Our Captain is the best commercial pilot in France and serves as chief
pilot for all the French companies.
He has also flown several times
across the Atlantic.
oür plane is
a very comfortable 15 seater (held
down by the mail load to only five passengers) trimotored, all metal
Devotine.
My fellow passengers are all an interesting lot. One is an engineer for
the Sperry Gyroscope Company•
His name is Zand - a naturalized American
born in Poland.
His father was Dutch, his Mother French.
raised in Switzerland.
He fought for
France in the world war and holds
five different decorations given to him during the war. Another passenger
is from St. Louis - where he has lived for several years - connected with
the Shell Petroleum Corporation. His name is William F. Court.
Another
Shell man from the East
and a representative of the Gruman Aircraft Com-
pany complete the list.
Now, at 9:45, we have just flown over Cadiz (our French pilot doesn't
seem to have too much respect for the soverignty of Spain), with Seville
off in the distance, well back from the coast. Then we passed Gibraltar

- 2 -
- quite close - it was a great sight - great banks of white fluffy clouds
to the east, floating lazily against a powder-blue sky,
while as a "back
drop" high snow covered ranges.
In the harbor behind
Gibraltar we counted
fifty ships - some men of war,
but mostly freighters - which had been
headed in there no doubt for examination of their cargoes by watchful
British patrols. We circled and in doing so passed directly over the
fort which stands off opposite Gibraltar in Spanish Morroco.
Then we flew straight across the blue Mediterranean over a convoy of
eight freighters headed in our direction, possibly also bound for Oran.
We arrived there at 11:10, and, much to my surprise, Oran is a modern
city with many ten to 15 story buildings, fine parks, apartment houses
and public buildings. The airport is an enormous flat plane surrounded
by hangars large and small - twenty eight of them in all - with foundations
completed and steel on the ground for many more.
It is here in North
Africa that France receives the planes purchased in America, and where
she is training her rapidly expanding air force. We went to a little
bar where fifteen or twenty French officers were loitering.
Behind the
bar a typical old Frenchman said "oui oui" when Dr. Zand asked if U.S.
dollars were good.
The young officers were playing slot machines around
the walls, while on a table in the middle of the room were a few hunks of
French bread and a plate of cheese.
We had dubonnet - five glasses for
proprietor didn't offer his customers more than the "merchant's lunch"
above described! Two officers at the bar - fine looking fellows -
asked us where we were from and were very much interested to learn that
we had come over on the Clipper.
They said the weather was exceptionally
cold for Alrica - sounded just like the Californians. It was cold - an
over coat would have been very comfortable.
We got away at 11:50, and now,
it is 12:30 and we are out
again over the Mediterranean flying directly across to Marseilles where
we are due at 4:30, but may be late on account of the inevitable head
wind. Off to our left in the haze of the horizon is the coast of Spain.
3:00 p.m.
This flight has been a real treat.
We have flown the whole
length of the Spanish coast and now have passed the French border.
of us are the snow-capped Pyrinees, rising majestically against a
pale blue sky. We are flying over a large bay now, direct to Marseilles
- looks as though we'd be ahead of time.
Later - Paris - January 17th.
At Marseilles we learned that our request
by wire from Lisbon for reservations on the Wagon-Lits to Paris was non-
productive.
Accordingly we squeezed on to a second class coach and had
to sit up all night.
There were seven in the compartment and sleep was
difficult, but, after only two hours of "shut-eye" the hight before, I
did manage to put in a few uncomfortable hours of "cat naps". We arrived
in Paris
yesterday morning and I never felt anything as grand as the hot
bath which was my immediate objective. Had dinner last night with my
friends from the Clipper and our Paris representative.
Paris seems quite
different in the semi-blackness of the partial black-out.
Everything
closes up at 11:00 p.m. and so I got to bed early and slept until 10:00
o'clock this a.m. Have an appointment for lunch and several more for

- 3 -
this afternoon, so will mail this opus.
H.M.B.
P.S. H.M. is now in Rome - has been in Zurich, and maybe
he is coming back next week.
E.C.B.
